title: Late blight disease in outdoor tomatoes

Header: Late blight disease in outdoor tomatoes
Phytophthora infestans Bakajani chelewa in Swahili

Prevention: Keep wide plant spacing (> 60 cm, 25”) to improve aeration.
Support plants with sticks, and prune plants for better aeration.
Disinfect knives and hands with bleach before working on next plant.
Wear gloves or wash hands with plenty water afterwards, because bleach is toxic.
Remove tomato residues and left over solanaceous plants, such as
Irish potato, pepper, nightshade and eggplants.
Plant away from infected fields and from
Irish potato, nightshade and pepper fields.
Avoid planting during wet and cool periods.
Preventatively spray 0.5 kg ash mixed with 1 litre fresh milk and 10 litres water at dry weather conditions.
Monitoring: Late blight is a fungus-like mould disease.
Search for small, water- soaked, greyish green, irregular areas on leaves.
Later the areas become dark grey and enlarge over entire leaves.
Underside leaves, a fuzzy white fungal growth might be seen in mornings or after rain
When you see stems turning brown to black, or fruits with large brown leathery areas, it is too late for action.
When dry weather is expected, some infection symptoms might be tolerated and infected plant parts can be removed.
When wet, cool weather (< 24°C) is expected, 2-4 plants with symptoms per ¼ acre are enough to consider quick action.
Direct Control: Remove and destroy whole plants when diseased.
Carry materials away from the field in a closed container such as a plastic bag to prevent the spread of the disease.
Mix 1 tablespoon baking soda with 1 tablespoon of vegetable oil and 4 litres water, then add 1 tablespoon soap, stir, use immediately for spray.
Finely chop 20 garlic cloves, soak 1 d in 100 ml mineral oil, then + 10 ml soap, stir, + 2 litre water, stir).
Spray over plants max 2x in min 7 day interval.
Mancozeb combined with copper oxychloride, copper hydroxide or metalaxyl
Chlorothalonil products ( Rav, Bravo, and others)
